title: Making Kubernetes AI-Ready for NVIDIA Vera Rubin on Day One | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's open-source AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) v1.0.0 ships Preview Kubernetes recipes for Vera Rubin NVL72 that passed deployment, conformance and a first cross-node NCCL all-reduce gate (744.71 GB/s busbw at 16 GiB) on early silicon. The post details the GB200-to-Vera Rubin upgrade deltas (new R615 driver branch, ConnectX-9/BlueField-4, changed NIC topology) and flags that inference performance validation is blocked because vLLM images are not yet built against CUDA >= 13.4.

themes.theme: Vera Rubin NVL72 upgrade deltas vs GB200

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 is the third generation of NVIDIA's MGX rack-scale architecture, an evolution of the same design used by GB200 NVL72.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Rack-level continuity eases customer migration from GB200 to Vera Rubin.
insights.quote: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 is an evolution of the same NVIDIA MGX rack-scale architecture, now in its third generation

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 requires a new GPU driver branch: it was validated with the host-installed R615.23 open driver, with early support targeted for R610 and official platform support in R620, versus an R580.173.02 baseline for GB200.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Official Vera Rubin software support lands with R620; current builds are pre-release.

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 replaces GB200's ConnectX-7 NICs and BlueField-3 DPUs with ConnectX-9 SuperNICs and BlueField-4 DPUs, with DOCA 3.3.0 being the first GA release supporting ConnectX-9.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Networking content per rack shifts to next-gen NVIDIA NICs/DPUs, an attach-rate tailwind for NVIDIA networking.

insights.claim: A Vera Rubin NVL72 compute tray exposes eight ConnectX-9 PCI device groups with 32 functions, compared with four ConnectX-7 adapters on a DGX GB200 NVL72 tray, though both trays have two CPUs and four GPUs.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Higher NIC density per tray implies more networking I/O per GPU and new affinity tuning for RDMA/GPUDirect Storage.

insights.claim: Rubin GPUs introduce new Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) profiles, but the AICR Vera Rubin recipes use whole-GPU allocation and MIG on Vera Rubin is not covered by the validation.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: GPU partitioning for multi-tenant inference on Rubin remains unvalidated at the Kubernetes layer.

insights.claim: GPU telemetry from early Vera Rubin hardware still reports a placeholder product name ('NVIDIA Graphics Device') that will only resolve once PCI IDs are allocated near general availability.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Signals Vera Rubin is still pre-GA as of this writing.
insights.quote: Note the placeholder product name, which resolves once PCI IDs are allocated near general availability

themes.theme: AICR recipes as Day-1 readiness tooling

insights.claim: NVIDIA positions the AI Cluster Runtime (AICR), part of the DSX AI Factory Platform, as the way to make Kubernetes environments ready for Vera Rubin NVL72 compute trays on Day 1 by capturing tuned configurations as reusable, versioned recipes, generating deployment bundles and validating live clusters.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is shrinking time-to-revenue for new GPU racks by owning the software bring-up layer, deepening lock-in.

insights.claim: Configuring Kubernetes for new GPU hardware is error-prone because drivers, kernels, runtimes, networking, operators and schedulers must be co-tuned, and small mismatches can prevent workloads from running or cap performance.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Software integration is a real bottleneck on GPU deployment ramps.
insights.quote: Small mismatches can prevent workloads from running or limit performance.
insights.locator: Configuring and optimizing Kubernetes for new GPU

insights.claim: The first AICR deployment on a never-before-validated combination (arm64, Ubuntu 26.04, 64k-page kernel, RKE2, Vera Rubin) went from cluster handoff to a healthy runtime in hours, and a second Vera Rubin cluster reproduced the result the next day.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Repeatable recipes could compress cluster bring-up from weeks to hours for neoclouds and hyperscalers.
insights.quote: that repeatability is the point and benefit of the recipe
insights.locator: The first deployment of this bundle

insights.claim: The Vera Rubin recipe family ships as Preview, without the production support and lifecycle qualification of a Supported recipe, because the platform itself is still pre-release.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Production-grade software for Vera Rubin is not yet declared.
insights.locator: The new Vera Rubin recipe family

insights.claim: The resolved Vera Rubin training recipe layers five overlays into 14 components, including GPU Operator, the DRA driver with ComputeDomains, DraNet, KAI Scheduler, NVSentinel, NodeWright, NFD and the Prometheus stack.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's own software stack spans scheduling, health monitoring and node tuning around its hardware.

insights.claim: Platform floors encoded in the recipe include Kubernetes >= 1.34.1 (for the GA resource.k8s.io/v1 DRA API and containerd 2.1 on RKE2), Ubuntu 26.04 with a Vera-optimized arm64 64k-page kernel, and raising the NFD topology updater's 60Mi memory limit, which gets OOM-killed on multi-terabyte NVL72 workers.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Vera Rubin effectively forces upgrades to the newest Kubernetes and OS stacks.

insights.claim: The full AICR sequence of recipe, bundle, snapshot and deployment plus conformance validation completes in about five minutes on a live cluster, and a two-node IMEX ComputeDomain goes from apply to running pods in about 12 seconds.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Fast, automated validation lowers the operational cost of standing up AI factories.
insights.locator: Going from apply to two running pods

insights.claim: On Vera Rubin NVL72 reference clusters with GPU Operator v26.7.0 and DRA driver v0.5.0, the training recipe passed all deployment, conformance and performance checks, including the first cross-node NCCL all-reduce over multi-node NVLink at 744.71 GB/s bus bandwidth at 16 GiB.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: First public multi-node NVLink performance datapoint on Vera Rubin silicon.

insights.claim: Early validation rounds were blocked by a hardware/fabric issue that kept one compute tray out of the NVLink fabric, resolved only after the hardware was reseated.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Early rack-scale bring-up still faces physical fabric issues, a potential source of ramp friction.
insights.quote: Bringing up new silicon is a process.

insights.claim: Running AICR validation surfaced an unmapped Rubin architecture value in go-nvlib that crash-looped the DRA driver's kubelet plugin; the fix went from first crash report to a validated build in about three days and shipped in DRA driver v0.5.0.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Pre-GA silicon still exposes stack-level bugs, but NVIDIA's fix cycle is fast.
insights.locator: The bring-up also worked in both directions

insights.claim: Architecture support flows from go-nvml into go-nvlib and then into the GPU Operator, Kubernetes Device Plugin, MIG Manager and DRA plugins, so a single low-level fix propagates consistently across NVIDIA's Kubernetes stack.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: A layered dependency chain means new-architecture readiness hinges on the lowest bindings.
insights.locator: Because architecture support lands first in go-nvml

insights.claim: Validation showed a host-managed IMEX daemon and DRA-managed ComputeDomains cannot share a node today, feedback that shaped the alpha host-managed IMEX option in DRA driver v0.5.0.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Operators must choose one IMEX ownership model per node when deploying multi-node NVLink.

insights.claim: Inference serving performance validation on Vera Rubin is deferred because although vLLM merged Rubin (sm_107a) support in v0.27.0, the SM107 kernel path requires CUDA >= 13.4 while vLLM's published images through v0.28.0 still build against CUDA 13.0.3.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Out-of-the-box open-source inference on Rubin lags the hardware; early inference benchmarks may be delayed.
insights.quote: So even the newest vLLM release image carries the dispatch code without the compiled kernel.

insights.claim: NVIDIA Dynamo's latest release (v1.4.2) pins vllm-openai v0.26.0, which predates Rubin support entirely, and its unreleased main branch pins v0.28.0, which is not built against CUDA 13.4.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: NVIDIA's own inference stack is not yet Rubin-ready, a watch item for inference ramp timing.

insights.claim: The authors argue a credible Vera Rubin inference-performance floor needs a published CUDA >= 13.4-built runtime image verified on real hardware, past the JIT-compile crash and not merely past a version check.
insights.speaker: Mark Chmarny
insights.so_what: Skepticism warranted toward early Rubin inference claims not backed by such images.
insights.quote: past the JIT-compile crash, not just past a version check
